```{=html}
<div class="term evi fragment" data-fragment-index="2">evidence <span>P(off)</span></div><div class="cell fragment" data-fragment-index="2">¾&middot;⅓ + ¼&middot;⅔ = <b>5&#8260;12</b> <i>&asymp; 42%</i></div><div class="cell fragment" data-fragment-index="2">P(do(off)) = ½&middot;⅓ + ½&middot;⅔ = <b>½</b></div>
<div class="term pos fragment" data-fragment-index="3">posterior <span>P(monsoon | off)</span></div><div class="cell fragment" data-fragment-index="3">¾&middot;⅓ &divide; 5&#8260;12 = <b>⅗</b> <i>&ldquo;off&rdquo; lifts ⅓ to ⅗</i></div><div class="cell fragment" data-fragment-index="3">½&middot;⅓ &divide; ½ = <b>⅓</b> <i>the prior again</i></div>
<div class="term sli fragment" data-fragment-index="4">so, slippery <span>P(slippery | off)</span></div><div class="cell fragment" data-fragment-index="4">⅗&middot;67% + ⅖&middot;3% = <b>41%</b></div><div class="cell fragment" data-fragment-index="4">P(slippery | do(off)) = ⅓&middot;67% + ⅔&middot;3% = <b>24%</b></div>
</div>
```
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.72em;margin-top:0.2em;"}
- Inside each season the panels agree; only the **weights**, P(season | off), differ
- Randomization's likelihood ratio is 1: **posterior = prior**, even for unrecorded causes
:::

::: {.notes}
The engine under the garden, in the Bayes' rule we met with the Bayesians — same colours on purpose: each row under the mosaics is one term of the formula, coloured to match. Ask the room one question: you walk past and see the sprinkler off; what have you just learned about the season? Read the See mosaic first, where every rectangle's area is a probability: the widths are the seasons over the whole year, the heights are the gardener's habit, and the outlined cells are the off days. Then click through the rows, one term per click, See on the left and Do on the right. *Prior*, P(monsoon): a third on both sides, straight off the calendar — June to September is 122 of 365 days. *Likelihood*, P(off | season): this is where they part. The gardener switches off on three-quarters of monsoon days and a quarter of dry ones — the hidden mechanism from the last slide, in numbers — and that ratio of 3 is how much "off" says about the season. Randomization switches off on half the days whatever the season: ratio one, it says nothing. *Evidence*, P(off): every way of getting "off", added up — the outlined area. Five-twelfths for the gardener; for randomization, P(do(off)) is simply a half. *Posterior*, P(monsoon | off): the monsoon's share of that outlined area. The gardener's "off" lifts a third to three-fifths — Bayes' rule done with rectangles; a random "off" leaves it at a third, the prior again.

The last row is the law of total probability — the same "average over the hypotheses" as the Bayesians slide, with the seasons as the hypotheses and the posterior as the weights. Monsoon days come with rain, the yellow, so 41% of the gardener's off days are slippery for reasons that have nothing to do with the sprinkler; when randomization sets it — written do(off) for that reason — it is 24%, a fair sample of the weather. Click, and land the two lines. First: inside each column the yellow share is identical in both mosaics — 3% and 67% — so seeing and doing agree about every season; they disagree only about the weights. That is why recording the season works. Second, the one to land: a random "off" tells you nothing about the season — or about anything else, including the causes nobody wrote down. That is what randomization buys. If someone asks about April or October: they are in — the dry season here is all eight months outside the monsoon, which is why it rains on 3% of its days, not none. Then click on for the three ways side by side.
:::

---

## Why Randomization Works

::: {.whyrand}
:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}
```{=html}
<p class="lede">Every Mumbai day, 1961–90: the true rates</p>
<table>
<thead><tr><th></th><th>dry season<span>Oct–May</span></th><th>monsoon<span>Jun–Sep</span></th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr class="src"><td>share of the year <span>calendar</span></td><td>&frac23;</td><td>&frac13;</td></tr>
<tr class="src"><td>it rains <span>real record</span></td><td>3%</td><td>67%</td></tr>
<tr class="src"><td>gardener waters <span>assumed</span></td><td>75%</td><td>25%</td></tr>
<tr><td>slippery if sprinkler on</td><td>100%</td><td>100%</td></tr>
<tr><td>slippery if off</td><td>3%</td><td>67%</td></tr>
<tr class="eff"><td>sprinkler&#8217;s effect</td><td>+97 pts</td><td>+33 pts</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
```
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{=html}
<div class="way see fragment"><p class="t">See <span>season not recorded</span></p><p>P(monsoon | off) = &frac35;, by Bayes</p><p class="calc">100% &minus; 41% = <b>+59 pts</b> <span class="no">&#10007;</span></p><p class="why">thirty years of data didn&#8217;t fix it</p></div>
<div class="way adj fragment"><p class="t">See + record the season <span>adjust</span></p><p>compare inside each season, weight by its share</p><p class="calc">&frac23;&middot;97 + &frac13;&middot;33 = <b>+76 pts</b> <span class="ok">&#10003;</span></p><p class="why">only for causes you knew to record</p></div>
<div class="way do fragment"><p class="t">Do <span>at random</span></p><p>P(monsoon | do(off)) = &frac13;, the prior</p><p class="calc">100% &minus; 24% = <b>+76 pts</b> <span class="ok">&#10003;</span></p><p class="why">balances causes nobody recorded</p></div>
```
:::
::::
```{=html}
<p class="formula fragment">see &nbsp;&sum;<sub>s</sub> P(y | x, s) &middot; <b class="b">P(s | x)</b> &emsp;&emsp; do &nbsp;&sum;<sub>s</sub> P(y | x, s) &middot; <b class="o">P(s)</b> &emsp;&emsp; <span>seeing weights by the posterior, doing by the prior</span></p>
```
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.72em;margin-top:0.15em;"}
- **Adjusting** fixes the confounders you know; **randomization** fixes them all
- To do experiments and find cause, you need a body
:::

::: {.notes}
The synthesis — the Bayes slide showed the mechanism; this puts the three ways to the answer side by side. Every number here comes from thirty years of real Mumbai rain (NOAA's Santacruz station, 1961–90, a rain day being at least a millimetre), so these are probabilities, not a sample — the noise of the twenty-four days is gone, which is the point. The whole year is in: the dry season is every month outside the monsoon, October to May, two-thirds of the days, and it rains on 3% of them — mostly October and November, the monsoon's tail. The only made-up row is the gardener's habit, and the only assumption is that wet grass is slippery.

Walk the table first. Inside a season, the sprinkler's effect never changes: in the dry season it is nearly the only water there is, +97; in the monsoon it mostly adds to rain that was coming anyway, +33. Then one click per card. *See*: Bayes said the gardener's off days are three-fifths monsoon, though the monsoon is only a third of the year, so they look slippery anyway and the sprinkler seems worth only +59. Stress that thirty years of data did not fix that — more data shrinks noise, not bias. *See, and record the season*: now you can fix it on paper — compare inside each season, then weight by how common each season is, two-thirds and a third: +76. That is Pearl's adjustment formula, and it works — but only for the confounders you knew to write down. *Do, at random*: +76 without knowing anything about seasons. A random draw cannot see the sky, so on days and off days get the same mix of seasons — and of every other cause nobody thought to record.

The formula line is the last slide in one row: seeing weights each season by the posterior P(s | x), doing by the prior P(s); randomization makes them equal, adjustment swaps them by hand. If someone asks why not just set the sprinkler by hand: you can, but if you choose by looking at the sky you are just a second gardener — randomization is what guarantees the choice is blind. Then land the last bullet slowly; it is the hinge of the back half — you cannot randomize what you cannot reach. That is why Section VIII turns to bodies.
:::

---

## VII. What We Want from AGI {.section-divider}

---

## Generality, Efficiency, Reasoning

- **Generality** — competence transfers to the untrained
- **Sample Efficiency** — human-like, from few examples
- **Robust Reasoning** — multi-step, causal, self-correcting

::: {.notes}
First three requirements. Generality means competence transfers to tasks it was never trained on — the opposite of the brittleness in Section VI. Sample efficiency is the spine's yardstick again: human-like learning from a handful of examples, not millions. Robust reasoning is multi-step, causal, and self-correcting — the System 2 the models still lack. Point out each one is a direct answer to a gap named earlier; this isn't a wish-list from nowhere.
:::

---

## Memory, Grounding, Aligned Autonomy

- **Persistent Memory** — no catastrophic forgetting
- **Grounded World Models** — causal, ideally embodied
- **Autonomy + Alignment** — open-ended yet controllable
- The last is a constraint — and the highest-stakes one

::: {.notes}
The remaining three, and slow down on the last. Persistent memory means no catastrophic forgetting — the missing piece from "The LLM." Grounded world models means causal, ideally embodied understanding, which sets up Section VIII. Then the crucial asymmetry: alignment isn't another capability, it's a constraint on all the others — we want open-ended autonomy that stays controllable. It's the only item where getting it wrong is catastrophic rather than merely disappointing, which is why it carries the most weight.
:::

---



## VIII. The Future {.section-divider}

---

## Foundation Models Meet Robotics

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="58%"}
- Model "brains" in capable "bodies"
- Surgery, deep-sea exploration, autonomous logistics
- The loop closes: sense → predict → act → learn
- Where the next decade concentrates
:::
::: {.column width="42%"}
<a href="https://www.unitree.com/g1" target="_blank" rel="noopener" style="text-decoration:none;"><img src="images/humanoid-robot.gif" style="width:100%;max-width:340px;border-radius:10px;display:block;margin:0 auto;"/></a>

<div style="font-size:0.3em;opacity:.55;line-height:1.2;text-align:center;margin-top:0.3em;">Unitree G1 — a body waiting for a better brain</div>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
This is where I place my bet on the next decade. Let the robot loop — it is a Unitree G1, a genuinely capable body you can buy today, and it is the point of the whole slide: the hardware has arrived, the brain has not. Sensorimotor competence is nearly solved; what it lacks is the grounded, causal world-model from Section VI. That gap is the bet. Put the foundation-model "brain" into a capable "body" — surgery, deep-sea and space exploration, autonomous logistics. The unifying idea is the closed loop: sense, predict, act, learn — which is Friston's active inference and the RL loop from Section II, now running in the physical world. Tell the candidates plainly: this is where I'd concentrate, the convergence of foundation models and robotics. But hold it lightly — a bet, not a prophecy.
:::

---

## AI Ethics — Beyond My Expertise

- **Cheap Dopamine** — engineered attention capture
- **Economic Effects** — labour, wealth concentration
- **Children** — growing up AI-saturated
- **Distribution** — who reaps the fruits of the technology
- A prior, held lightly: fewer regulations tend to serve better

::: {.notes}
Handle with humility — say out loud that this is outside my expertise, because it is, and the honesty matters more than coverage. Name the stakes without pretending to resolve them: engineered attention capture ("cheap dopamine"), labour disruption and wealth concentration, children growing up AI-saturated, and who actually captures the benefits. The regulation line is a personal prior, explicitly held lightly — flag it as a view to argue with, not a conclusion, and invite disagreement in the discussion. Don't linger or preach.
:::

---

## Key Takeaways

- "AI" is an ambiguous term — today it means LLMs
- Minds run on prediction — octopus to cortex to transformer
- Human intelligence is the ML task list, written first in our biology
- The open gaps — reasoning, memory, grounding, alignment — are the agenda

::: {.notes}
The recap — tie the spine threads together one last time so they leave with them. "AI" is ambiguous and today means LLMs; minds run on prediction, from octopus to cortex to transformer; human intelligence is the ML task list written first in biology. Then land the fourth bullet as the handoff: the open gaps aren't failures of the field, they're the research agenda — reasoning, memory, grounding, alignment. Slow down; this is the last content slide — let the fourth bullet be the closing line, then click once to the Thank You slide and open the floor there.
:::
